cases.title: A fatal test-vehicle crash exposed gaps in oversight
cases.eventPeriod: 18 March 2018
cases.summary: An Uber developmental automated vehicle struck and killed a pedestrian in Tempe, Arizona. The NTSB identified the distracted safety operator as the probable cause and organisational safety shortcomings as contributing factors.
cases.aiRole: A developmental automated driving system controlled the vehicle. The finding covers human oversight and safety management as well as automation.
cases.affected: The pedestrian killed in the crash and people exposed to testing on public roads.
cases.outcome: The NTSB issued a safety investigation report and recommendations. This record describes the safety finding, not a criminal verdict.
cases.limitation: A fatal crash cannot be attributed to AI alone. The official finding names multiple contributing factors.
cases.lesson: A human backup only helps when the whole system supports effective supervision.

cases.title: Public photos became a facial search database
cases.eventPeriod: Collection and Canadian services investigated in 2020–2021
cases.summary: Canadian privacy commissioners found that Clearview collected sensitive biometric information without consent and violated federal and provincial privacy laws. The service matched faces against images scraped from the internet.
cases.aiRole: Facial recognition made scraped images searchable by a person's face.
cases.affected: Canadians whose images were collected, including children.
cases.outcome: After the joint findings, three provincial authorities issued orders in December 2021 to stop specified services and non-consensual collection, use and disclosure, and to delete relevant images and biometric data.
cases.limitation: This describes the Canadian findings and December 2021 orders, not the current status of every later appeal or proceeding. Clearview disputed the original findings.
cases.lesson: A photo being publicly visible does not automatically mean consent for biometric reuse.
